speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED REFUSAL OF MINISTER TO DISCUSS FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether he would care to comment on the reported statement of the premier of British Columbia that while in Vancouver recently he, the minister, had been invited to discuss federal-provincial financial arrangements for the Columbia river project and had not replied to the invitation which, no doubt out of respect for my hon. friend's favourite procedure, was sent to him by telegram.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPORTED REFUSAL OF MINISTER TO DISCUSS FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
If that is the report in the press it is not a completely correct report of what happened. I was in Vancouver last week on the Sunday and Monday. I had previously addressed a letter to the premier of British Columbia suggesting that it might be advisable for representatives of the department of the provincial treasurer of that province and of the federal Department of Finance to meet at a mutually convenient time to discuss any questions related to the financing of the Columbia river development that might be appropriate.
I was on a quite tight schedule on that trip west. I was due to leave Vancouver early on Tuesday morning. At a very late hour on Monday night-indeed, just when I was in the act of packing in preparation to leave Vancouver-I received a telegram from the premier suggesting that I should go on to Victoria. It was quite impossible, of course, to do so at that time, as I was due to speak in Winnipeg the following day. I proceeded to Winnipeg, fulfilled my engagement there and returned to Ottawa on Wednesday morning. On my return on Wednesday I addressed 79951-0-263J
a letter to the premier explaining the circumstances and why it was quite impossible, under the circumstances, for me to accept his invitation at that time, but suggesting that when he returned from his trip to the United Kingdom, on which he was to leave at the end of last week, I would be happy to arrange for such a meeting at a time that would be convenient to him.
I do not of my own knowledge know this, but I am told that having dispatched this telegram to me on Monday-apparently late on Monday-he went to the radio or made a radio statement within a day or so complaining that he had not received any reply to his telegram and that I had not gone to Victoria. Under the circumstances, if he made any such statement, it was obviously entirely premature. I think it would have been the part of fair play to wait until adequate time had elapsed for a response to reach him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORTED REFUSAL OF MINISTER TO DISCUSS FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext: May I thank the minister for his reply and tell him I quite understand the difficulties of a tight schedule. Does he care to comment on the further statement made by the premier, namely that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) had already informed the government of British Columbia some time ago that the federal government would pay 50 per cent of the cost of this project but that, in the reported words of the premier of British Columbia, they have been running away ever since from that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPORTED REFUSAL OF MINISTER TO DISCUSS FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
To my knowledge, Mr. Speaker, my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not made any such statement to the government of British Columbia. There has been no running away from anything. It is not the practice of this government to run away from its positions, its statements or its responsibilities. I think this matter would be much better advanced, Mr. Speaker, to the mutual advantage of British Columbia and the rest of Canada if an effort were made to arrive at understandings of the positions of the two governments without rushing into radio or press reports, as apparently has been done in the quarter referred to by the Leader of the Opposition, and trying to make some political statement.
The fact of the matter is that there has been an exchange of correspondence on this subject with the premier of British Columbia. We have been quite clear in the statements

Inquiries of the Ministry we have made to him. The matter of the development and the sharing of cost has been discussed at the several conferences that have been held between representatives of the federal government and representatives of the government of British Columbia. At this very time a meeting is in progress at Washington at which both governments are represented in discussions with representatives of the United States administration on this entire problem.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think it is not inappropriate for me to say that there have been ample opportunities for discussion of this subject and that all the opportunities that are required will be afforded. There will be no running away from any responsibility on the part of the federal government. We simply ask that all those concerned approach this matter in the same understanding and co-operative attitude.

Mr. Speaker, in reply to questions by the hon. member for Kootenay West and the Leader of the Opposition, I should like to make a brief statement concerning the fingerprinting of public servants.
During the second world war members of the Canadian armed services were fingerprinted, primarily for purposes of identification. In the years following the war the Department of National Defence and a number of other departments and agencies initiated the practice of fingerprinting for those employees requiring access to classified information, as well as for certain employees responsible for the protection of public property.
In 1954 the previous government decided to extend this procedure to all persons employed in positions requiring access to classified matters, including certain persons employed in positions of trust although they might not have working access to secret and confidential papers. At that time the civil service commission was asked to provide the necessary facilities for taking fingerprints of these categories of civil servants at its offices here and across the country. Crown companies and agencies were asked to make separate arrangements for the fingerprinting of their employees.
Inquiries of the Ministry
There has been no change in this policy since its inception, and I should like to assure the house that it is not the government's intention to extend this procedure to all public servants.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last night, I had been giving what seemed to me to be the best reasons in favour of the immediate setting up of a national advisory board on economic development and trends, and automation.
It is quite obvious that the establishment of such a board is absolutely urgent. The main reason for it, in my opinion, is that the policy of the government, ever since it has been in office, has been one of makeshift and political expediency.
The creation of such an advisory board is, in my opinion, the most appropriate and efficient way to get us out of the economic deadlock in which we now find ourselves.
I submit there is no denial of the principle of responsible government, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) erroneously indicated last night, in the fact of seeking advice from experts; and I believe that if the government had adopted that policy two or three years ago, we would not now be in our present difficult situation. Not only is that advisory board advocated by Canadian newspapers, but it has also been many times endorsed by organized labour, as could be seen again this morning, in a release from the Canadian and Catholic Federation of Labour, which reads as follows:
The Canadain and Catholic Federation of Labour announced over the week end its intention to ask the federal and provincial governments to set up economic advisory boards to consider practical solutions to the unemployment problem.
That, almost to a word, is the very essence of the amendment put forward yesterday by the hon. member for Essex East. Such an advisory board would also meet the hopes and suggestions expressed by our hon. Conservative friends in 1954. In fact, it is seen on page 2085 of Hansard, that the Conservative opposition at that time suggested to the government that a review of the economic situation should be made in 1954 as a means of finding employment. And everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, that the situation in 1954 was in no way comparable to the present difficult situation.
I think it might be well to place on record the list of our Conservative friends who, in 1954, saw fit to suggest that we review the matter. On page 2564 of Hansard, I find the following names:
Mr. Balcer, Mr. Churchill, Mr. Diefenbaker, Mrs. Fairclough, Mr. Fleming, Mr. Fraser (Peterborough), Mr. Fulton, Mr. Green, Mr. Hamilton, Mr. Hees, Mr. 

Howe, (Wellington-Huron), Mr. Macdonnell, Mr. McGregor, Mr. Monteith, Mr. Nesbitt, Mr. Nowlan, Mr. Pearkes, the Hon. Mr. Rowe and Mr. Starr.
(Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I must inform him that his time has expired.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
Before commencing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a statement made last night by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, who has just taken his seat. At page 4168 of Hansard he made the following statement, and I shall read it in French: (Translation):
I should like to offer the Minister of Labour a challenge I wish he would take up one of these days. I wish he would attend a meeting in Montreal, for instance, where a third of all the unemployed in Canada are to be found, and deliver before those people the kind of speech he has made here in the house tonight.
(Text):
I think perhaps the hon. member is not in touch with what has been happening in Montreal, because I should like to point out to him that just two weeks ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), speaking to a group of labour leaders and union representatives in Montreal, made almost exactly the same type of speech that he made in the house yesterday, and he was greeted by applause from that group.
I should like first of all to examine the amendment with which we are now dealing. We are dealing with an amendment which is not quite a motion of non-confidence. There is, in this amendment, no condemnation of the government for anything it has done. It is merely a request or a suggestion that a committee should be set up. The hon. member for Essex East, after solemnly assuring the house that his amendment would not touch upon any matter that had been already decided by the house, nevertheless went ahead and made a long speech on unemployment, at the conclusion of which he proposed the motion to set up a committee to deal with the causes of unemployment. I would not accuse the hon. member of leading the house down the garden path, but he certainly did have me fooled.
I should like to have a look at the economic situation as it is in Canada today. I am positive that it is not as bad as it was painted yesterday by the hon. member for Essex East. We have to admit, Mr. Speaker, that in any expanding economy there are bound to be pockets of unemployment. This is caused by, among other things, the shifting and

relocation of industry. However, the hon. member for Essex East quoted yesterday from a dominion bureau of statistics report. I should like to refer to some of the items appearing in that report of Friday, May 20, 1960. The only figures to which the hon. member for Essex East referred were those relating to construction. I cannot find the figures to which he referred because in his remarks, at page 4132 of Hansard, he stated that construction starts fell by 35 per cent; that was for the first quarter of 1960.
Looking at the weekly bulletin of Friday, May 20 we find that building permits issued in March fell by some 14 per cent from a year earlier. I think it is fairly obvious why this happened. Parliament had not voted any funds until some time during that first quarter, so there were no funds available from the time the money voted for the previous year was exhausted.
However, there were other items in this bulletin to which the hon. member did not refer. The first is manufacturing. Manufacturers' shipments in March were valued at an estimated $1,959 million, some 7 per cent greater than in February and 3.5 per cent above the March, 1959 level. Merchandising; department store sales, during the week of May 7 were 6.1 per cent greater than a year earlier, while April sales climbed by 6.9 per cent. Agriculture and food; more creamery butter, Cheddar cheese, ice cream and skim milk powder were produced in April and January to April of this year than last. In so far as transportation is concerned, the number of cars of railway revenue freight loaded on Canadian lines in the week of May 7 rose slightly to 76,165. Manufacturers' shipments, inventories and orders; manufacturers' shipments in March were valued at an estimated $1,959 million, an increase of nearly 7 per cent from the revised average estimate of $1,837 million according to the latest dominion bureau of statistics figures.
Now, we can take any group of figures such as this and pick out one in which there is a decline, but taking the whole group as indicated in this latest weekly bulletin there has been a very definite increase all across the line in matters relating to the national economy.

There is no doubt at all that the pattern of employment is changing in Canada, just at it is in North America and elsewhere in the world. As automation advances the place of the unskilled workman in our economy is gradually lessening. It is 79951-0-264

Mr. Speaker, the amendment is not one for which I have any great enthusiasm, although my colleagues and I are going to support it. The reason it seems somewhat nebulous really lies, in my view, in the speech introducing it, in which the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), in a rather delightful wandering, much and often intercepted by irrelevant or at least apparently irrelevant points of order raised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), really did not fill us in on just what this national advisory board which he and his party were advocating would do. The motion reads in part as follows:
-a national advisory board on economic development and automation with representatives of governments, industry, labour, agriculture and universities,^-
While no mention is made there specifically of the provinces, they would have to come in. We are left, as a number of hon. members have pointed out, with the spectre of a board that would be rather large and perhaps unwieldy. I should like to have known whether the hon. member for Essex East contemplated something like the president's council of economic advisers such as the United States government has. I think we might have merited a bit more elaboration on how this particular board was to handle two items which, although related, seem to me to be quite different in scope and scale; that is, how it was to handle the question of economic policy, which is definitely a long term matter, and the question of automation, which is of not so great a theoretical scale and which surely will have to be faced by a series of short range steps. It seems to me that to give this suggested board those two particular functions could lead to a number of difficulties.
One word that is missing from this phrase "national advisory board," of course, is that magic word to which C.C.F. speakers usually give obeisance but which Liberal speakers


tend to shun. I refer to the word "planning". We are enthusiastic about planning, and it might just be conceivable that we are going to have a national planning board in the future. I do not know how long it is going to take; it will depend on the initiative, or lack of it, of this government. Perhaps a national advisory board would be a step along the way.
But irrespective of what the hon. member for Essex East did not say in letting us know what this board was going to do, we had a speech from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). One of the things that intrigued me about his responsibility is that he has given us what I think is the most forthright statement of any cabinet minister in Canadian history in that he has said that his government and he, in so far as his department is concerned, accept the responsibility for unemployment.
We have had in the past governments which have committed themselves. I refer especially to the Liberal government in 1945, which committed itself to a policy of full employment. But this is the first time to my knowledge, when I have ever been able to put my finger on it, that a minister has come right out and boldly said, "We accept responsibility". I think that is very much worth while.
But when we hear the minister talk we find that he gives us a picture that is rather radiant and sunny. It is as though his government has created a magnificent beach, and from one end of the beach to the other the water is warm, is at a consistently safe level, and you do not have to worry. But then he talks about problems. In other words in this nice beach, where the water is at an average level, delightfully tepid, and where you seem to be perfectly safe, there are a number of holes into which people can slip and drown. It is this kind of unevenness, these holes, that moves me to comment that I think we had every right to expect more from this government in the particular economic field than we have received.
As I said, the Minister of Labour is a particularly bothersome kind of personality to have been projected into this particular situation. We all admire him. We like the way we are treated. When you go to him or go to his office, you can get information. The other day he made reference to the fact when one of the Liberals raised the point that some unemployment insurance commission offices were no longer giving information to members of parliament, that he had provided it to me and to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai). This sort of thing

is commendable. We have the minister saying that his department accepts its responsibility. But what we have not got, Mr. Speaker, is any confidence that the minister either looms large enough in the cabinet or that this cabinet is interested enough in this particular problem, namely the problem of the developing unemployment crisis.
The minister quoted from the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. I think this is probably the most overrated commission that Canada has ever had. I would say the conclusions are almost useless with regard to any government planning. The minister quoted approvingly from the report those sections in particular that dealt with the optimistic picture. I would point out to the minister that although the conclusions of this commission are very much lacking in pungency, on page 426 of those conclusions the report states:
The fact of the matter is that the problem of preventing unemployment or of correcting a condition of unemployment once it occurs has not been fully solved. There are things which governments can do under such conditions and if they are done at the right time and with sufficient vigour and forthrightness, we may be hopeful, perhaps cautiously optimistic would be a better way to put it, that they will be successful, depending upon the circumstances at the time and particularly upon conditions and circumstances in the United States. But the business of influencing the level of economic activity in a country is a new art which is relatively untried. And there is nothing certain or foolproof about it.
I think most of us can agree with this particular conclusion; and reference is made to the fact that all the rosy predictions of the Gordon report rest on the assumption that we are not going to have any periods of severe cyclical unemployment. I do not know whether we have a really severe cycle in progress now, but I do know that as of May 5 in my own particular region, which is a prosperous one, over 15 per cent of the labour force were still seeking jobs and unable to find them. I think statistics generally indicate that we have a peculiar unemployment problem at this time, with high production but very many sore spots developing, and a very general level of unemployment that cannot be explained as frictional, that cannot be explained as seasonal and that cannot be explained simply as the result of technological change. My own assumption tends to place paramount the idea of technological change.
In my particular region, which runs roughly from Sudbury westward to the Manitoba boundary, we have the woods industry giving a rather buoyant economy at the present time. We have quite a number of mining prospects and mines in operation, and as we are in the nature of a bridge across central Canada we will always have a large number employed in 79951-0-2641
National Board on Economic Development the transportation field. In all three of our major industries, the pulp and paper industry, the mining industry and the transportation industry, immense amounts of capital have been inverted in recent years which have led to an unbelievable reduction in the working force; or if you want to put it another way, there has been an unbelievable increase in productivity.
I think this can best be seen in terms of the woods, where any woods manager today will tell you that with the equipment he has now he can cut three times as much wood with the same number of men as he could cut 12 years ago. Unfortunately there is neither the opportunity nor the prospect of increasing the cut of our woods so we can engage an increased labour force. Therefore we are left with the situation where the number of people needed in the bush is dropping, and dropping sharply.
Exactly the same thing is obvious to anyone who has followed the fortunes of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway; the railway employees are thinning out, and when central traffic control comes in, as it will within the next 18 months, the drop will be very pronounced.
As far as the mines are concerned the figures are not quite so startling. I can remember that at the first mine I worked there was an underground staff of approximately 100 to put up 400 tons of rock a day. I know one mine today in the same region which puts up over 3,000 tons a day with an underground force of 100. The picture we can see in our own particular region, and see it very startlingly and clearly, is that the kind of productivity increase which our large industries have been getting as the result of rather immense capital outlay has cut down labour opportunities. Of course in terms of gross size or growth capabilities or growth prospects, our future labour prospects are consequently deadened. It is impossible to build up a large population, even though productivity and the value of what we are producing is increasing, if your labour force is not expanding.
This particular condition which we suffer at the present time and which I think is going to increase highlights the need for some way out of the conundrum. We need some sort of study, co-ordination, planning, and then some kind of policy. I have no faith in this particular cabinet being able to get on top of this particular situation.

I remember that the hon. member sat in a committee I sat on and listened to one cabinet minister and several ex-cabinet ministers all say that they were far too busy to look after this and far too busy to look after that. That is one of the most unfortunate things about cabinet ministers today; they are loaded down with so much routine that these men-and I think many members of all parties share this view-have not the time to work out the kind of policy which we need.
It was mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) that this resolution indicates a lack of faith in our civil servants. I have slightly more faith in the cabinet than I have in senior civil servants so far as their being able to work out the sort of policy decisions of the overall kind which we need in order to confront problems like automation and unemployment. It seems to me that we need some kind of internal change in the cabinet structure and some way of developing economic advice which can be used by the cabinet at the top level. This is why this particular board which is proposed might be useful.
I think those people who protest that this is just another step of creeping socialism should remember that the United States president has had this type of counsel at least since 1948. His advisers publish quite a number of reports, and their annual forecasts are looked over by a great many people. I think we should also remember that in the United States, where they make a fetish of free enterprise and private enterprise and a free market, they still have a tremendous number of agencies, both governmental and foundation, such as the twentieth century fund and the international brothers fund, all working on economic problems and developing economic policy. It seems that we have only the occasional royal commission.
To underline the need for some kind of national co-ordination, I think it should be pointed out that we have information sources, in the dominion bureau of statistics of a statistical nature, and in the national research council of a scientific kind. I know we also have some of our more regulatory agencies, such as the atomic energy board, the board of transport commissioners, the maritime commission, the aeronautics board, the tariff board, even the Bank of Canada and the controversial Coyne. In all these agencies we have knowledge and expertise, and I suppose the possibility of policy development on the part of these people. But it seems to me that they tend to be isolated. Regulators tend to


short range, narrow decisions. They do not manage, co-ordinate or direct. There is little indication that any of these people are being brought together with other people outside of government, such as the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Labour Congress, to work out plans for meeting the type of problem which has been highlighted by this amendment.
An economist by the name of Berle recently pointed out some thoughts on planning which seem to me to be relevant here. In his book "Power without Property" he said:
The word "planning" has fallen into the lingo of stereotyped political controversy; you are for it as a solution; you are against it as a danger. Analysis of what planning is seems to be absent.
Certainly we talk grandiosely here in this house-and I am including Conservative backbenchers particularly, during the debate on the speech from the throne and the budget debate-about various aspects of planning, and all types of advice is given to the government urging them to do this and that. The author goes on to say:
Factually, planning is not a panacea and cannot be

We invoke the word "planning", but planning is not in itself going to solve everything. The writer continues:
It is a process by which solutions can be reached, not a solution in itself. Planning does not remove conflicts of interest. Each economic sector will struggle to attain the most advantageous position it can, and will not be vividly interested in the problems or difficulties of other sectors. Plans when made may be successful, or they may be hopelessly inept or oppressive.
What the planning mechanism does do is to supply a means and a method by which these conflicts can be resolved. The data on which plans are constructed necessarily forces consideration and development of principles on which conflicts may be resolved, and of criteria by which solutions may be judged, revised, or improved.
Then there is this sentence which seems to me to sum up what is taking place in the United States; I cannot see it on the horizon yet in Canada.
In economics we are slowly pounding out a sort of common law whereby conflicts of interest and moral claims of individuals may be resolved other than by brutal economic struggle.
In Canada we have always hesitated to face the consequences of the brutal economic struggle. We have today a royal commission sitting to study all the problems of transportation. This underlines how deeply the Canadian government has been committed over the years to policies of participation and intervention. We have the maritime freight rates; we have these Crowsnest grain rates which no one should really talk about because it is such a sensitive point; we have subventions for maritime coal; we have a

bridge subsidy to pay the railways for maintaining this expensive link across the country.
In connection with another aspect of transportation we find the trucking people appearing before the commission and asking for subsidies so that they too may get a share of the subsidy pie. We find the C.N.R. $50 million in debt in one year with no relief in sight in the future unless the prospects change substantially. We have the president of the C.P.R. going around and certainly not being optimistic about the future of his railway. All this seems to me to indicate that we need some kind of council, some kind of national focus. Perhaps this should be the cabinet at the present time, but I do not see how the cabinet is going to get to it. Despite the multiplicity of its sittings, where is the economic policy?
One thing which is so striking about the membership of this house, when one considers hon. members who do not come from the Montreal-Toronto golden triangle or quadrilateral, if you want to call it that, is that they all want secondary industry in their constituencies. Every time they discuss their needs among themselves, one hears this demand for secondary industry. In northern Ontario, western Ontario, in the maritimes, in the outlying parts of Quebec and on the prairies, everybody wants secondary industries. Yet there are no prospects at all for a large expansion of secondary industry in these parts of Canada and there will not be, in my opinion, until this government is ready to do something which the government of the United Kingdom has already done, namely bring in an establishment of industry act together with a definite policy of putting secondary industries into regions that are depressed or which have not enough job opportunities.
It is obvious that this government is not ready at the present time to make that kind of move, but it surely has to come. Surely this is the direction in which we have to go, and that is why there is a need for some kind of national economic board or national advisory board, as the hon. member for Essex East has put it. We know that such a board could get information on statistical questions from the dominion bureau of statistics. We also know that most of the provinces now have their own statistical bureaux. I think such a board could count on a great deal of help in research from the universities or from certain agencies in the universities. I believe we might expect the regulatory agencies which are already in existence, such as the board of transport commissioners, to be able to supply a certain kind of knowledge.
National Board on Economic Development But we badly need a means of bringing all this into focus, enabling us to develop a policy designed to meet these problems.
I do not wish to stray too far from this theme, but the problem of trade, for example, readily occurs to us. We have people in business associations going around the country clamouring for a change in our commercial policy, a change which would tighten it up. We know there are interests in the country which are very much against such a change, especially the people in the west. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken)-I think he was involved-has mentioned the disquiet in many people's minds about our educational set-up. The Minister of Labour himself not very long ago expressed chagrin and shock at the number of people who were leaving school too soon without the qualifications necessary to prepare them for useful careers. These are some of the problems we have to consider. There is also, for example, the question whether we should have shorter hours to work and get down to a 30-hour week; the question of the relationship of defence planning and defence production to our economic capacity, and so on. Consideration of all these questions needs some kind of strategy board, so they may receive the kind of attention and crystallization which the cabinet does not provide at the present time.
For instance, we were very anxious, when Canadian Car and Foundry in my own area suffered a serious blow when its commercial operations were switched to Montreal, that the company should have the opportunity to produce the Bobcat vehicle for defence use. However, many people who do not come from the lakehead are saying, why should we get into a venture of this kind, and how can you approve of the creation of this particular vehicle simply as a means of cushioning a particular community from the effects of unemployment or automation? I cannot conjure up an easy solution here. I know that every one of us becomes torn between constituency interests and the national interest. But surely, somewhere, someone should be considering questions such as this and giving advice with regard to them.
We are a number of years away, I should say, from the stage where we are going to have a national planning board whose plans would be automatically implemented. The Canadian tradition has been to appoint royal commissions and get indefinite recommendations, or sometimes definite recommendations, as in the case of the Rowell-Sirois commission, and then to implement pieces of those recommendations as the political and economic situation demanded or permitted. In answer to the hon. member's question, as I understand it the policy has been worked out mostly by politicians who recognized the need in northwestern England, in parts of Wales and Scotland, and have taken the lead.
I am speaking on the basis of a very biased article which I recommend to the hon. gentleman. The article is entitled, "The Apotheosis of the Dilletante" and is written by Thomas Balogh. It is an attack on British civil servants for being a bunch of mandarins who, by being all-around gentlemen, sort of crossword puzzle experts, have never got around to having enough expert knowledge in any one sector to develop or elaborate policy. I feel that this criticism can be applied to our senior civil servants. There may be some excellent all-arounders, but I do not know whether we have a sufficient concentration of special abilities in some kind of co-ordinate form that will allow us to develop really positive policies.
I know that hon. members on the government side of the house will argue that there is no need for this. One would assume there is not when one listens to the bland assurances of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour that everything is fine. Perhaps they are right, and it may be that time will prove them so. However, we do have enough serious problems in Canada to warrant this kind of thing. We have a country which in my opinion is economically more difficult to govern than Britain or the United States. I think it is time that our cabinet, our civil


servants and the best abilities we have in the country had some means of concentrating in order to develop the kind of reports and policy suggestions that the President of the United States, for example, gets from his council of economic advisers.
The need, of course, is urgent or less urgent, depending upon your political position and the region from which you come. I know it is fashionable, especially in the house and in the open, for hon. members of the government to express all kinds of compliments. One must give credit to the Minister of Labour, who has said that this government accepts the responsibility for the problem. The hon. gentleman has admitted that there are problems in various sectors, but on the other hand he frequently tells us that everything is fine. I suggest to the minister that the unemployment problem is building up. We must recognize that a large part of our working force in Canada is becoming permanently unemployable. We therefore have to get to the roots of the problem very quickly. I do not have confidence in the minister's civil servants being alive to the problem and doing something about it.
Another question that comes up in any consideration of Canadian economic problems is where do the provinces stand? The mari-times, through the Atlantic economic council, are complaining about the monetary and fiscal policies of this government and urging that there should be some way of developing policies to help regions like the maritimes. We have had strong indications of the feelings and problems of the prairie farmers. We also have had on the part of secondary manufacturing industries a demand for change in our commercial policies. The situation in our mines and forests does not compare favourably with that of even two or three years ago. Looking ahead we can see that these industries will be in serious difficulty unless action is taken. This is especially true of the pulp and paper industry, which faces the threat of Russian competition.
With all these manifold problems which Canada has always faced but which in my opinion it faces today in a more acute form through increased competition, it is time to take action. There is the germ of a suggestion here upon which I should like to see the government act.
One of the points made by the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects with respect to the whole question of economic planning and development is this:
The whole matter is further complicated by the very important part which public confidence has to play. If businessmen and investors are confident and optimistic, it should not be hard for governments to encourage expansion of economic activity.

We are beginning to get indicators in this area. We know that a large part of the money for our expansion has come from the United States, but we see indications that this source is beginning to decline. We have the problem of the outer seven and inner six in the European common market. We have the age-old problem of inflation. We have the Minister of Public Works being so bold as to say, in effect, that this government is not going to take exceptional action this year in order to bail out the construction industry, which is facing problems and predicaments; yet that industry is crying and howling long and loud at the present time. We know that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has expert knowledge in this field and a body of facts available. I also imagine it has a policy that might be fitted into a larger picture, but we have no idea what is being done to elaborate that policy.
A few weeks ago I talked to a veteran newspaper man who spoke about the changes that have occurred since this government took office. He said that a newspaper man always looks for the source of power. If he finds it in a certain place he can put his finger on the pulse, as it were; he can formulate a conception of what is in the wind, what action the government will take in certain areas, and find answers to his questions. He said that when the Liberal government was in power there were two or three places you had to look. You had to check the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance and usually the prime minister's office. The interesting thing he finds about this government is that now the real pressure is brought to bear in one central place. If you want to find out what is or what will be cooking you go to the Department of Finance.
To someone listening to this statement this will seem to be a natural situation. It would seem that this should be the department where major decisions are taken. I suggest, however, that the Department of Finance will tend to make most of its decisions negative ones because of the very nature of the relationship of the treasury board and the fact that the Minister of Finance is the budget master who is always concerned with things along that line. I do not want to suggest that this department should not be a large source of power or that decisions should not be made by the man who is in charge of the budget and keeping our monetary affairs in balance; but if that is where the main source of power lies at the present time I venture to suggest that we will have a negative attitude, one that will not enable us to develop positive policies to meet the
National Board on Economic Development wide range of problems we hear mentioned by practically every hon. member who speaks in this chamber.
For this reason I suggest that the time has come to implement a proposal similar to that made by the hon. member for Essex East. The way the hon. member outlined it, I fear there would be created far too big a board or council to be effective at the start. One thing I would hope for from such a board is that the government would stop trying to represent every region, every ethnic and religious group and every branch of industry in the country, and that kind of representation mania. Surely we are at the stage where there are men in Canada who are big enough and able enough to rise above the limitations of ethnic or religious considerations or an industrial or labour background and serve as a small council of economic advisers who could be of genuine assistance to the government, and especially the cabinet in working out economic policies to enable them to face the diversified range of problems we have in Canada.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce are not organizations which you readily think of as sitting down amicably together in a given situation; yet if you read what all three organizations have been saying recently you will see that they have been asking for something like this. I really thought the lion had laid down with the lamb a few months ago when I learned that the financial editor of the Globe and Mail advocated some sort of over-all planning board. He emphasized that it is necessary to parcel out capital requirements for certain developments in the future so there will not be too much competition among the various branches of industry. When you have very large agencies such as the labour congress and the manufacturers' association beginning to see that we cannot meet the gigantic problems facing us without some form of co-ordination I think it is time for us to start looking at our own federal government, the role it plays and the liaison with provincial governments.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has insisted that the government accepts the responsibility for a national economic policy. I think it is time for them to say how this responsibility is going to be met and I think it needs to be met by more than platitudes or the general bland assurance that under this government everything is great. We will be watching very closely to see how much power is given to the Minister of Labour and what changes he will make in order to carry out the indications he has given

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) accused the government of belittling the problems facing our economy and of not being concerned with a variety of problems affecting unemployment, exports and imports, agriculture, housing and railways. As already mentioned in this debate, the government is aware of and is giving close attention to the problems in all segments of our economy. To solve these problems the opposition has introduced an amendment advocating the setting up of a national advisory board on economic development and automation with representatives from different bodies with the aim of developing economic policies designed to achieve a high and stable level of income and employment. No one will disagree with the objective of the opposition but I believe that the method suggested in order to arrive at a solution is not the proper course to follow. I have been searching for words to describe the Liberal opposition and have found them in the statement that they are a quixotic government with a quixotic mind.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the results obtained speak for themselves, and that is just what I was referring to a few moments ago. In 1935 the Conservative government brought in an unemployment insurance measure. Was it not the King opposition that claimed it was unconstitutional? After the Liberals came to power in 1935 did they not take six years to bring in the Unemployment Insurance Act even though they had claimed that the Conservative legislation was unconstitutional? As already stated by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), did it not take the former minister of national health and welfare 20 years to bring in a national health insurance plan? Yet this same gentleman stands up now and expects the present government in the short period of two years to cure all the ills caused by their administration. I believe it took the dark, the bleak, the dull days they have spent in the opposition to lighten their intelligence.

I will abide by your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I should like to consider the effects of these different measures taken by our government to aid our economy. The output of steel has been higher than the final two months of 1959. The steel mills in the first weeks of May have turned out 120,240 tons of ingots as compared with 110,803 tons a year ago. Shipments of iron ore during March totalled 219,619 tons as compared with 190,601 tons a year ago. Then, 90 per cent of the department stores dealing in various commodities find their position improved by as much as 5 per cent to 13 per cent as compared with a year ago. The effect all this has had on our export and import trade can be gauged by looking at the statistics for the first quarter of this year which show that exports were valued at $1,219 million, 22.8 per cent higher than the corresponding period last year and imports were valued at $1,330
National Board on Economic Development million higher by 9.3 per cent than a year earlier. Thus the imbalance in the first quarter of 1960 was sharply reduced to $38.7 million from the $166.2 million in the same period of 1959.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, these have been the measures which this government has taken to give a lift to our economy. This has not been done through the creation of boards and commissions, irrespective of the assurance which the opposition gives that results can be obtained in that manner. I believe that the creation of too many boards and commissions is conducive to excessive bureaucracy. We must admit that we have inherited too many boards and commissions from the Liberal party. Very often these boards and commissions bring forward the ills from which our economy is suffering in their true light, but they always leave it to the government policymakers to initiate the methods by which these ills may be cured. Excessive bureaucracy may lead, and has led to indifference amongst business people toward political life.
Our government must, therefore, approach these problems of the present and the future in a business way, and not in a manner that will result in an excess of reports and red tape. We should actually adopt business methods to apply at home as well as abroad. When I refer to "abroad" I may remind hon. members that the methods adopted by the Department of Trade and Commerce are proving worth while today. I spoke about realism and the lack of practicality which is apparent in the opposition. They remind me of people who may be standing knee deep in the December snow while speaking about this year's tulips.
The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) mentioned yesterday that the core of the problem was in finding ways of attracting capital to Atlantic provinces enterprises. When a businessman contemplates undertaking a new business does he not consult industrial experts, export and import experts and financial institutions capable of advising and guiding the prospective entrant into new fields? No true Canadian is dependent upon others to tell him the type of business in which he should indulge because he is quite capable, as time has proven, of finding his own field of activity. However, he needs counselling and this government has set up the necessary machinery to give information to those who may desire it. It would be a sad day when any government would say to an industry, you will locate in this particular area; you have no choice in the matter.
However, I agree with the hon. member for Gloucester when he speaks about the

These and many other things mentioned by the hon. member for Gloucester have been the ways and means this government has adopted to help the economy of the Atlantic area and those engaged in the fishing industry. I will repeat that this does not represent all that is required, but I believe that anyone will realize that a government cannot accomplish everything within the short period of two years. The steps taken so far will, I am sure, prove fruitful to those engaged in fishing on the Atlantic coast.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I make reference to those divisions within the departments which bring help and information to those who require it in their attempt to bolster our economy. However, there are a few other words which are necessary, and they are those which should be addressed to industry, to labour and to management: Work harder, co-operate more and bargain harder.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with only part of the remarks just made by the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Keays). He blamed


the Liberal party for taking six years to set up the unemployment insurance commission.
If he had gone a little deeper into the matter, he would have seen that, as soon as the question had been submitted to the supreme court, and the latter had rendered a decision in October 1937, on November 5, 1937, the Canadian government submitted to the provincial governments a plan asking for authorization to set up an unemployment insurance commission to settle all problems that might come up from time to time.
He would also have found out that all provinces agreed, except two, those of Mr. Aber-hart and Mr. Duplessis. It was only after Mr. Duplessis' defeat in 1939 that the Ottawa government was able to secure provincial assent.
It shows that, in this as in other respects, the Ottawa government wanted to respect provincial rights and that is what kept the unemployment insurance commission from being established sooner.
And heaven knows what dreadful predicament workers who are now unable to find employment would be in but for that commission.
Mr. Speaker, may I therefore, right at the start of my remarks, be allowed to offer my congratulations to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr).
The speech he made yesterday is probably one of the best ever heard in this house. He sought to indicate that everything is rosy and, with much ponderation, artful dodging of difficulties, and very skilful play upon words, he attempted to show that the problem is not so very important.
I may say that, for a good while he certainly managed to create that impression. It was therefore the most skilful speech he has ever delivered, and for all my being in the opposite camp, I cannot do otherwise than congratulate him and tell him, even though I do not share his views, that I enjoyed his speech tremendously.
I said a moment ago that he had played upon words. He did, and most adroitly. For instance, in referring to increased benefits, he managed to drag in the question of fishermen, and in such a way that we could readily suppose that the Conservative government had extended unemployment insurance benefits to them.
Yet, as administrative head of that department, as the man upon whom rests the great responsibility of seeing that the unemployment insurance act is applied, he knows better than anyone that it already existed when

he took office, that it was under a Liberal regime that unemployment insurance was granted to Canadian fishermen, and that if fishermen did not come under the act-our national economy being somewhat upset as you will admit, Mr. Speaker,-they would be in an appalling situation, as are in any event the other sectors of our economy.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: Because of the Liberals.

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext:
Liberal members recognize facts as they are; as for Conservative members, who refuse to admit that everything is going wrong at the present time, they will learn about it at their own cost at the next federal election.
Meanwhile, I shall go on with my remarks.
Speaking about the amendment, the minister said this: "This government does not intend to set up committees in order to shirk its responsibilities". And he added: "It would be a cabinet outside the cabinet".
Now, Mr. Speaker, would it be the first time that this government has resorted to a group of experts to look into some particular problems? I doubt whether we could find another government which has set up a greater variety of commissions, about everything and nothing, as this one has done so far. However, all those commissions that were set up were perhaps designed for the legitimate purpose of helping definite areas or special sections. What we want is a type of organization that would make regular and detailed investigations and advise the minister and the government with regard to their problems. Would the minister be afraid, for instance, that such a commission of experts might arouse him from his lethargy, in the same way as the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Coyne, tried to rouse the Minister of Finance? He would be in great need of this, if we are to judge by his actions so far and the results he is now getting.
We admit, as everybody must, that the employment situation in Canada is probably the worst we have had for a very long time.
And the minister added: "What would such a committee do?" The answer is very simple. The committee might undertake a complete inquiry on economic conditions, which could be of help to our leaders. Indeed, as the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said a few moments ago, our ministers are overworked, have too much routine work to do, and probably have no time-as I fully realize-to go deeply into the situation.

Have they, in their respective departments all the necessary experts available for this type of investigation? I doubt it. And even if various specialists were available in those departments, they are civil servants, and today officials are afraid to give frank and honest opinions because of the attitude taken by the government with regard to suggestions made by Mr. Coyne, governor of the Bank of Canada. Those people are afraid to open their mouths. However, if we had an outside group of experts, they would have greater freedom for a serious study and might offer some suggestions. It would then be up to the government to find out what was fair and reasonable for this country.
Such a commission might look into the employment situation and, not being connected with the government, they would have no interest in whitewashing every action taken by this administration. Then again, being no part of the opposition, they would have no interest in belittling government action. They would be independent of those contingencies. So, after a thorough-going study of the situation across Canada, they could advise the Minister of Labour who, in the presence of undeniable facts, might be in a position, if he himself has not the power to legislate, to try and convince his colleagues in the cabinet to do something about it. They could consider the particularly complex problem of unemployment, for unemployment is practically permanent at this time, and does not seem to fall off even in the summertime. Then too, there is seasonal unemployment, which requires an altogether different approach. A commission such as this independent of both the government and the opposition, and made up, not of civil servants but of employees who need not tremble at the frowns or thunder of either the minister or the Leader of the Opposition, might manage to come up with concrete, considered recommendations of such a nature as to help this government which, heaven knows, certainly needs help at this time.
For instance, it could consider the fact that men are being gradually replaced by machinery. The hon. member for Port Arthur said a few moments ago that, for the last 12 years, only half as many men as before are needed in the lumber industry. In the pulp industry and paper mills, new machines are so efficient that, in paper making for instance, only three men are now needed where 18 used to be required. Everything is done by machinery. There are devices that show where a break can occur. All the operator has to do is to push a button; the machine
4190	HOUSE OF
National Board on Economic Development stops, the repair is made, and the machine is again set in motion. Thus, in many cases, a man has only a few hours of actual work to do in a whole year, and this creates a new problem that must necessarily be solved. We cannot ask the worker himself to solve this problem; because it is not his doing. So, we must ask the government to consider the situation. But, as the hon. member for Port Arthur said, the government has no time for it, nor have the Ministers of Labour, of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) or of Finance (Mr. Fleming). Still, someone has to do it. The only people who could have time to consider it would be those men that we could pick and single out for their special qualifications in different fields of the economy and, in this way, make up for the ministers' own lack of time by making suggestions to improve the situation.
Such a commission could find remedies that could become permanent features. But no, when we talk of a committee or commission or board, it is rejected by the present government, which has perhaps appointed- at least to my knowledge-more commissions than any other. Could it be because the suggestion comes from the ranks of the opposition?
The minister said yesterday; we have read the suggestions put forward by the opposition. We are considering them. It will probably take over two months to implement them.
However, we are dealing here with something positive that does not commit the government. The government can appoint an advisory board, but it does not have to accept its recommendations. The government could later consider what had been recommended by a group of men in a position to advise. Why is the government against this? Why did the Minister of Labour, last night, try to minimize the importance of such a board? It is beyond me. This is not a motion of want of confidence in the government. I realize that the motion would raise a problem that the government could not accept. I would say that on the political side, perhaps something can be done. We are just suggesting this: that the government itself set up this commission of experts to make a study in that direction. The Minister of Labour has thought fit to say that he does not want a 

government within another government. I cannot recall any advisory board having been in the nature of a government within a government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow me a question?

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: How do you explain that, under the previous government, when there was a fairly acute unemployment problem, no commission was appointed along the lines suggested by the hon. member?

subsubtopic: BOARD ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND AUTOMATION
speechtext: There was an unemployment problem at the time the Liberals were in power. As I said, the Liberals have not always had it soft. They have known difficult times. However, the unemployment problem which faced them in 1953 and in 1955 did not deteriorate to the point it has reached in this country today. At that time, we had in the cabinet men like Mr. C. D. Howe, for instance, who, on finding that our United States market was declining, toured Latin America, starting with Mexico and went deep down into South America, showing those people, with the help of our industrialists that Canada was able to produce many commodities they needed. I remember perfectly that, immediately after the visit, that is, in the fall of 1955, Canada was flooded with orders. As a matter of fact, the wheels began to spin so fast that, in 1956, we were favoured with a very prosperous year, thanks to the efforts and prestige of the men who formed the Liberal cabinet.

speechtext: Therefore, according to you, a commission such as the one you have been talking about would have been a good thing to have set up under the former administration?

Mr. Speaker, I admit that such a commission would have been a good thing; I recognize it today.
I agree that it would have been a good thing even at the time of the Liberals. However, if at that time the Liberals felt they had no need for it, is this a good reason why this government should turn down the suggestion from Liberal ranks at a time when we are facing the worst situation ever known in this country?
It has also been stated by the Minister of Labour that the income of workers had reached an all-time high. Perhaps it has, in some cases, but certainly not in the case of civil servants. We are told of record salaries; well they have to be record salaries, in the light of the increased cost of living between 1959 and 1960.
According to D.B.S. figures,-and I shall not quote those of 1952-53,-for 1959-60, we note that the cost of food has increased by 1.6 per cent; of housing, by about 3 per cent; of clothing, by 1.2 per cent; household appliances, by 1 per cent. The cost of other services has gone up from 133 to 137 per cent. Of course workers need record wages to meet those growing costs.
The minister added that employment had reached its highest level, but if we consider the continual increase in population,-a yearly increase of 600,000,-and if we take into account an increase of about 100,000 workers, is that comparable to the increase of population? No. There is a normal increase, a natural one, which occurs under any government, be it Liberal, Conservative, C.C.F. or any other; it is the increase in population. It is necessary that it should be so, but what about those who are out of work? That is the question which the hon. minister did not answer. Yes, what about those who have no jobs? Are they happy at the thought that nothing seems to be done to help them?
Yet, Mr. Speaker, those people would be very happy to know that the government has accepted some suggestion, even one coming from the opposition, in order to find a way of solving almost permanently the problem which is causing them to suffer today. Now, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex East is precisely aimed at giving special help to those who are suffering the greatest hardship in this country.
My last reference to statistics will consist of figures published in the Labour Research bulletin, under the heading "Unemployment again, unemployment still". We find that the people hardest struck by those conditions in this country are, first of all,
National Board on Economic Development the Atlantic provinces as a whole, which have 18.3 per cent of Canada's unemployed; Quebec comes second with 15.6 per cent, while British Columbia has 9.7 per cent of this country's total of unemployed, the average percentage throughout Canada being 10.7 per cent.
It has been said, and newspapers have repeated it, that when the figure is higher than 3 per cent, conditions are abnormal. Well, Mr. Speaker, we are certainly facing an abnormal situation, one which demands an outstandingly vigorous policy if we want to try and settle the issues we face at this time.

The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Essex East is precisely the remedy we need to end this situation. Canada's unem-loyed-particularly in large cities, when they are now reduced to begging-would be very pleased to see the government accept this

amendment. They would see a ray of hope in the fact that the government, which so far has been unable to cope with the unemployment situation, is calling upon experts to try to find a way out.
Mr. Speaker, while hundreds of thousands of workers are walking the streets, seeking employment, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough)-I am coming to the point-authorizes the publication of advertisements such as that one in a Belfast newspaper, where jobs are being offered to accountants, aerodynamicists, architects, beauticians, bookkeepers, cashiers, bricklayers, butchers, meat cutters, etc. The list goes on and on.
As evidence of the inconsistency of the government's policy, here is something that happened recently. A gentleman from Hull, a meat cutter with years of experience, called on me and asked me to help him find a job. Confident by reason of the fact that the department of immigration, presumably in co-operation with the Department of Labour, had been advertising jobs available in Canada, this gentleman, as I say, sought my help in finding a job. Quite pleased at the prospect, I wrote the following letter to the minister:
The Hon. Michael Starr,
Minister of Labour,
Confederation Building,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Minister,
When I received a copy of the invitation to come to Canada, extended to several trades in Belfast, Ireland, by the Minister of Immigration I wondered whether we really had no Canadians able to fill at least some of those jobs.
In the list, I find "butchers and meat cutters", and I know that the unemployment insurance office does not seem to be aware of any scarcity in this trade, because Mr. Rene D. Lamothe, 135 Montcalm street, Hull, who has 25 years experience in meat cutting and slaughtering, and who is now in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits, has not been offered this type of employment.

I shall be looking toward to an early reply.

Mr. Speaker, that is the reference I was making. To substantiate his assessment of the weakness of our economy the hon. member for Essex East referred yesterday to imports. He did not say that the position was weak with regard to exports. He simply said that there are indications of elements of strength in our export situation. He thought he was making a great concession, but after saying that he went on to say, "But can these increases in our exports during recent months be maintained"?
Certainly the export picture right at this juncture is very good indeed. In every succeeding month since September of last year there have been increases in the volume and value of exports, and during the first quarter of 1960 exports reached a figure of over $1,200 million. That was an increase of some 22 per cent over the corresponding period of 1959.
At the same time our imports, it is true, increased but they increased much less rapidly than our exports. Our imports increased by 9.3 per cent and therefore our import imbalance picture improved very substantially in the first quarter of 1960. The import imbalance is down now to some $38 million whereas it stood at something like $162

National Board on Economic Development million lor the first quarter of 1959. Surely such astounding progress, on the one hand a 22 per cent increase in exports and on the other hand only a 9 per cent increase in imports, is not a basis for pessimism and is not a basis upon which the hon. member for Essex East can come to the conclusion that we are faced with this great, this terrible weakness in our economy, a weakness which I suggest lies more in the arguments of the hon. member. That was one of the points upon which his amendment was based.
He also picked out certain other elements where he felt there were weaknesses. Before we come to that I should like to say a further word about exports. Many people have been, and I suppose justifiably, asking themselves, what is going to happen next? Our exports have been holding up well. They held up well in 1958 which according to everybody was a depression year. However, there was no significant drop in our export figures for 1958. There has been a substantial increase in those figures for 1959 and today we are starting a new year. We have completed one quarter of that new year and we have chalked up a record in volume and value of exports.
In view of that encouraging picture can we be satisfied that there is reason for the anxiety and gloom exhibited by members of the opposition? When I hear these members of the oppositon speaking I am reminded a bit of a bunch of spoiled children. They have had everything that their little hearts could desire, but they are not satisfied because they think that sometime in the future perhaps things will not be as rosy. I believe that is a correct appraisal of the attitude which these hon. members have adopted. When we look at our export situation we can see important problems developing, perhaps as some have suggested through the formation of trading groups in Europe or the emergence of a new industrial trading giant such as Japan. It is up to the people of Canada, under the leadership of the government as that leadership is being provided now, to find a solution to these problems and assure that the progressive trends in our export trade will continue.
There is, as people know and will readily admit, great prosperity in Great Britain and in the countries of western Europe. These countries have become so prosperous in recent months that they have lifted import restrictions. They have gone all out to increase their volume of trade. I submit that this provides another great opportunity to our Canadian exporters to fulfil the needs of the people of these countries who are now prosperous and who are now increasing their standards of living to a degree they have never
[Mr. Martineaui
experienced before. Instead of looking at our export figures and asking whether or not they will be maintained, I submit that hon. members of the opposition would be better advised to try to point out to the people the true facts and the unparalleled opportunities for greater sales which would result in greater progress in Canada. I must say, therefore, that in so far as the weakness in our export trade is concerned as mentioned by the hon. member for Essex East, that weakness exists only in his own imagination and in the fallacy of some of his arguments.
Again I must say that the hon. member picks out of our whole economic situation a few choice items such as construction, and he seemed greatly perturbed about the fact that construction was going downhill. In the last week's issue of the Financial Post, I have just seen the report of the MacLean building survey. According to that survey there has been an increase of 26.5 per cent in all types of construction as compared with the first quarter of 1959. This report admits that during the first quarter of 1960 residential starts were down as compared with last year. It was stated, however, that this decline was more than offset by progress in industrial, engineering and commercial construction. I say again, therefore, that when the hon. member for Essex East bases his amendment on weakness, he must look elsewhere than in the construction field. And so it goes all along the line.
The hon. member mentioned, for instance, that there was a decline in the output of automobiles during one week. It is, of course, quite understandable that he would be interested in this subject because he represents a Windsor constituency. He just picked out one week. I was looking at some of the automobile production figures, and I found that in March there had been a substantial increase in production over 1959. There is no doubt that 1959 was a year of great recovery, and there is no doubt that 1960 will be a record year. The Financial Post as late as last week stated that all indications, taken as a whole, pointed to the fact that 1960 will be a record year unequalled by any of the past years, including all of the great years of prosperity, so-called, which my hon. friends say occurred under their regime. The Financial Post has not, as yet, revised its opinion. The article stated that this record year would be experienced by most firms in most industries. Now that was quite a sweeping survey of all spheres of activity, and after making adjustments for some declines in certain fields, it is stated we will have a record year.
In so far as residential construction is concerned, according to the latest survey there

will be a marked improvement as more and more conventional lenders come into the field. The hon. member, therefore, was giving a very shaky reason for the establishment of that much vaunted national advisory council which he recommends in his amendment. If we look at the recent speech made by the president of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, Mr. A. C. Ashforth, we find that he says the year 1960 will see a contained boom in Canada. There is every reason for optimism concerning economic conditions in this country.
I do not want to burden you, Mr. Speaker, or the house with a long series of statistics. However, everywhere we look we can see indications that 1960, presenting as it may formidable obstacles, will chalk up new records which will be the result of the industry of the Canadian people supported by vigorous leadership as exemplified by the present government.

speechtext:
I have mentioned that
before and I am going to mention it again, Mr. Speaker. I am glad my hon. friend mentioned unemployment. I treated a bit of it at the start of my speech. However, a certain phrase used by the hon. member for Essex East struck me forcibly because it stirred vague memories of its having repeated many times in the past. With a great show of concern and with his face wrinkled by the preoccupations which he felt-and which I have every reason to believe were sincere-he said, "We now have a hard core of unemployment in this country". He said that as if he were finding something that came from high above, as if he had received some sudden inspiration on the spur of the moment as to this hard core of unemployment in this country; and he spoke in such terms as to lead this house to believe that this was recent invention and that it had been invented by the present government.
I was a bit curious about that reflection and I went back a few years. I happened to be reading a speech made by no less a personage than a former minister of finance of this country, a highly respected man; I refer to Mr. Dunning. This speech was so enlightening that I believe it merits quoting here. I refer to Hansard of February 25, 1937, page 1217. These words were uttered by Mr. Dunning, the then minister of finance, in his budget speech of that year:
Still more disheartening to most observers is the failure of the numbers on relief to decline proportionately with the revival of business ... However. to those observers who look for an early end to the relief problem the decline during the past year will appear discouragingly small.
National Board on Economic Development
Then he went on to say this:
It is probably true, Mr. Speaker, that a hard core of unemployment and relief will always remain.. . Even in the best of times, we have always had unemployment, but the unemployed have not been "in the statistics" nor a charge upon public funds to the same extent as today.
There you have it, Mr. Speaker. In 1937, not under a Conservative administration but under the great Liberal regime, almost two and a half years after it had taken power in 1937 on the promise that it would solve once and forever that great problem of unemployment, the minister of finance of that day admits tragically to the house that there was then a hard core of unemployment and that it would remain with us in the best of times. Yet today members of the opposition come here and say, "We have the answer to that hard core and the answer lies in the establishment of a national advisory commission".
That proposal may seem fairly sensible to a great many people. Certainly on its surface it looks to be appealing. But again I think it is always a good thing to look back into the record in order to see whether similar situations have ever existed previously and whether similar remedies were applied and, if they were applied, what were the results.
We remember 1935. We remember the great campaign carried on that year. It was an election year and Mr. King rode back into power on the promise of solving that big unemployment bug which was then plaguing the country and with regard to which no session passes without ample reference being made. His remedy to the problem was precisely the establishment of a national employment commission. That sounds very much like a national advisory council to look after full employment, automation and related problems. Hence one of his first gestures after assuming power was to bring forth that child of his brain which he had long nurtured.
It is extremely interesting to follow the progress of that commission throughout the years during which it worked. First of all, we have its establishment in the early part of 1936; I believe it was January. It was established then. That was already six months after it was promised but nevertheless it was established and persons were named to this commission and were supposed to get to work. When Mr. King made his much heralded promise during the election campaign of 1935, he pointed to an unemployment figure during that summer of 1935 of some 400,000 persons.
