speechtext:
We are getting there presently. If you take one thing at a time you never go wrong. I can understand the impatience of hon. members opposite in skipping those years. They always want to have this country believe that unemployment was a problem which was created in 1930 and which promptly came to an end with the ascension to power of that great Liberal regime in 1935. But let us face the facts as they are. If we analyse correctly the performance of our economy and the performance of the past administrations, perhaps we shall get to the root of the problem and find the correct answer. I am making my speech now. The hon. member has made his speech. He had his little say. Now let me have mine.
So, Mr. Speaker, we are back in 1937; and in that year in parliament there were many queries as to that famous national employment commission that had been set up. On going through the record we find that by the middle of 1936-oh, the commission had done a great deal of work-the government had issued 35 orders in council whereby they appointed all sorts of people and bought all sorts of the most modern equipment of that time to launch their famous commission. In 1937 parliament again convened. There was a debate on this national employment commission and we find that the unemployment figures were stable. In 1938 we find the same thing again; it is repeated all over again. It is on the record. If hon. members care to look it up they may read the debate on the national employment commission and get the facts.
By 1939 this commission had been in existence for three years. Up to that stage it had spent in excess of $325,000. I should like to point out that this was a formidable sum, even by today's standards. In those days it represented a substantial portion of the government's revenue. They had spent that sum and finally they came out with a report. The commission was established on the assumption that it would be an indefinite commission. It was not formed for any special time. It was something which most observers thought would last forever or as long as that government existed, at any rate. But by 1939 the Liberal administration was so proud of its infant that it promptly disbanded the commission entirely as soon as the report was out. The report was tabled in the house with great fanfare and then quietly and promptly buried and forgotten.
Of the many recommendations which were contained in the commission report, none was enacted in that year, 1939. Here we are in the fourth year after the Liberal regime, the men who were going to cure this


great unemployment problem. They had this commission and at the same time unemployment continued its same course of stagnation and was as much a serious problem in 1939 as in 1935. As a matter of fact-these figures are all contained in the record-by January or February of 1939 there were over one million people receiving relief in Canada. This despite the four years of that great administration which was going to cure unemployment and which had devised that child brain of its leader, their great unemployment commission, to solve that problem once and for ever, eradicating it from the face of our national economy.
Mr. Speaker, in the face of that remarkable performance can we take seriously the amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex East? First of all he bases his amendment on the great deteriorating state of the economy-which facts and figures prove to be otherwise-and second he proposes a remedy that has already been tried. When that commission sat for three years and tabled its report no step was taken to improve the unemployment situation. So I can only conclude that this amendment is certainly not a remedy in 1960. I have full confidence in the measures that this government has taken, is taking now and will take in the future to meet the problems of the day as they arise. In 1957 everyone said we were in a recession. The year 1958 was supposed to be a recession year. Our government did take certain measures. As hon. members know, they increased by a substantial amount the money supply. Government expenditures were vigorous and pronounced. Taxes were reduced. These measures were all adopted by our administration and as a result recovery was initiated in 1958. In 1959 when the corporations, businessmen and the population at large were engaged in the performance of the year that was just ending, everyone agreed it was record year in almost every phase of Canadian activity.
I am telling you that to show the hon. members that this government has taken measures. Some of them were said to be very vigorous. They were all adopted and they were all appropriate to the needs of the times. And they all performed their useful function, namely putting an end to the Liberal-induced recession and bringing back a period of prosperity which we have enjoyed and which we will continue to enjoy.
Hon. members say that in 1960 things are pretty good but there are clouds on the horizon and things will not be quite so good later on. I have full confidence in what has been done. This government has advisers; it has economists; it has whole armies of people who are taking the pulse of the

economic life of this country and who are suggesting to the government the measures which should be taken. Our government has the responsibility of decision. When the facts are before the government the government will act. Past performance is a gauge and guarantee of future success in solving these problems.
I just want to leave one parting thought. The government has shown that it will take every measure that a government can take to restore confidence in this country, but in the last analysis success or failure depends not on the many speeches which have been made here either on one side or the other. It reposes in the determination of the people themselves, in their confidence. I think that we should reflect on what has happened in Europe after the last war and how Great Britain has recovered. I was in Britain during the last war as were many other hon. members here, and we all know how they faced problems which had no comparison with the present problem facing our own country today. Britain and other countries in western Europe have staged a dynamic recovery despite great odds. Is it unreasonable to assume that if our own Canadian population, which has received so much in the post-war decade, not so much because of what the government might have done but simply because of a variety of circumstances beyond our control, were faced with obstacles it would not rise to conquer those obstacles so that our chart ahead would be one of continued and solid progress? That is why I think that this amendment is only another one of these smoke screens and must be dismissed. Let us get down to some serious business.

This was pointed out by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Thrasher) recently when he said in a speech that there were cases of fraud being perpetrated against the Unemployment Insurance Act.
But this does not mean, as some supporters of the government are trying to convince the people at large at the present time, that anything like the bulk of those who are registered for employment in this country are slackers. Far from it. The large majority of the people registered for employment at the present time are honest, industrious people who ask nothing else than the opportunity to go to work and to earn for themselves their daily bread. That is a right which we could not deny them. It is a right which we cannot afford long to deny them.
As I said before, there are several factors involved in this unemployment situation. There is unemployment which has been called seasonal, and that which is known as frictional which occurs when a person leaves a job and is waiting to find another. There is also the hard core of unemployment which has grown up in the last two or three years and which seems to have been caused by automation. Then there is, perhaps, unemployment from other causes. We know this is a complex question, but we do know one thing else, and that is that this government has no solution and that its actions have not been equal to coping
4200	HOUSE OF
National Board on Economic Development with the situation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said in this house on January 19, 1959:
We have with decisiveness met the problems as they have arisen. We intend to continue to do so. We realize the unemployment problem as it is. We have acted. We are now criticized for having acted, in effect, because, having placed $750 million in one stream, namely the housing plan, naturally there would be inflationary influences. I believe our first responsibility is to assure that everything will be done in order to meet the situation of those who, by reason of conditions over which they have no control, find themselves unemployed. That is what we have done. We did it in connection with the unemployment insurance. We extended the period. We did it in connection with the winter plan. We have done it in connection with housing, with public expenditures and with public works. That course we intend to follow in the days ahead.
Whatever the course that has not been followed; whatever the plan that has not been successful; whatever the government has undertaken has not been good enough, because the problem today is as bad as it ever was. In fact, it is worse in its effect than at any time since the thirties. In determining the nature of this problem it is necessary to obtain as much additional information as possible. Again, if I may, I should like to quote, this time from the Globe and Mail of February 19, 1960. This is from an editorial which reads, in part:
So who is unemployed, and where and why?
This is the point, and this is the question all parties should ask if unemployment comes up for general discussion in the commons today. It is not a matter of opinion but a matter of fact that Canada has chronic labour shortages in several fields at this time in occupations which require high skill or training. This newspaper is willing to accept it as an equal matter of fact that Canada has temporary or chronic labour surpluses in certain other fields. Which are they? If we knew precisely what skills were in shortage and to what extent; if we knew precisely what skills were in surplus and to what extent, we could discuss unemployment, and act upon unemployment, more intelligently both inside and outside parliament.
Surely a break-down could be obtained without too much difficulty. Surely a census could be made of those who are registered as seeking employment. We can find out who they are by age, by training, by experience and by any other category which might be felt to be helpful toward determining a solution of this perennial problem. If, at the same time, those who are unemployed but who are not registered were asked to do so for the purpose of the breakdown, an accurate picture of the problem would emerge. Next year the decennial census will be taken. This involves the asking of questions in relation to 18 million people. I suggest it would not be difficult to take a census involving some
800,000	people. This should be done at once without further delay, because the information is badly needed.


In the meantime, some things are obvious even to casual observation. The government's program-if one can dignify it by calling it a program-has been inadequate. The winter works program was too little and too late. It was discriminatory in its application.

Mr. Speaker, before six
o'clock I had started to mention a number of suggestions that I thought might be conclusions of a national advisory board if one were established. The second suggestion is portable pensions. It seems to me that this is not only an obvious but also an essential development. I was talking to a man a few days ago who was seeking employment. He had been turned down by one automobile manufacturing firm, by one rubber manufacturing firm, by one agricultural implement organization, by one electrical manufacturer


and by one government. He was turned down in every case for the same reason, because he was too old. He was in his mid-forties. What a travesty, Mr. Speaker, what a waste and what a heartbreak. This man is disillusioned, disappointed and has lost his reason for existence.
The next suggestion has to do with fiscal and monetary policies. There have been too many gyrations. The management of our economy has not been smooth enough. Far too much new money was created in 1958 and then none in 1959. Why? Was it because of government pressure? What was the reason for the tight money policy last year? Was there a shortage of goods and services?
Mr. Pallet!: Will the hon. member give the amount of new money created each year, if he is going to make that statement?

The hon. member can look that up for himself. In 1956 there was a shortage of capital goods, capital goods which were being used to increase the industrial capacity of this country and to provide additional jobs for Canadian workers. But this was not so last year. This was not the case. What was the reason then? Was it fear of inflation? Was the government afraid of the so-called wage-cost cycle? If so, it has not said so. We do not know the reasons but we do know the results. The provinces and municipalities had to borrow abroad. Many necessary local projects were postponed or cancelled. Was the danger due to the actions of this government the year before or were there other factors we have not been told about?
Another suggestion is the increasing of our export sales abroad. Some Canadian manufacturers seem to prefer an exclusive jurisdiction within a small limited market rather than seeking a part of a world-wide market. We as Canadians have to become better salesmen. We have to go out and try to sell our products abroad. Our trade commissioners do a very worth-while job and are most competent people but they cannot substitute for hard salesmanship. Recently a Toronto publisher was telling of a trip he had taken abroad. He expressed the opinion that if Canadian manufacturers really applied themselves and sent trained and skilled salesmen around the world looking for orders they could increase Canadian sales of manufactured goods two or three times in a very short period.
Another suggestion, Mr. Speaker, is aid to our tourist industry. There should be loans to establish new tourist facilities. I am sure that many members have had the experience of talking to United States visitors to Canada

who were not impressed with the accommodation and food they had found in certain localities in our country. I was also surprised this afternoon that the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) did not mention this when he was speaking.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that there should be accelerated depreciation for equipment and research designed to facilitate winter employment. May I recapitulate these suggestions? They are: (1) A massive scheme of technical training and retraining; (2) a system of national portable pensions; (3) a sound fiscal and monetary policy; (4) the encouragement of export sales of Canadian manufactured goods; (5) the guaranteeing or otherwise providing of loans to build up a greater tourist industry; (6) the acceleration of the completion of the trans-Canada highway for the same purpose; and (7) the allowing of accelerated depreciation for equipment and research to facilitate winter employment.
These are just samples of the type of suggestions a national advisory board might make. This is a time for action. It is futile for government supporters to attempt to bring into the present situation the alleged opposition of the Right Hon. Mackenzie King to Lord Bennett's proposed unemployment insurance legislation. As a matter of fact, for the benefit of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Keays) and the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau), may I say that as soon as the court decided that Lord Bennett's unemployment insurance legislation was ultra vires Mackenzie King wrote to the provincial premiers on November 5, 1937 asking them to agree to a constitutional amendment. Mr. Duplessis refused. It was not until the Liberals came into office in the province of Quebec in 1939 that consent was obtained and the Unemployment Insurance Act was then promptly established. What a mess we would be in today without it. Even this act, which is now due for an overhaul on the basis of experience, is not sufficient for today's problems.
The situation continues to deteriorate. There is much public concern as evidenced

Surely this is sufficient reason, Mr. Speaker, to justify the setting up of the proposed national advisory board. We have heard some strange statements from ministers during this session but perhaps none stranger than that of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) last night indicating the government's opposition to the appointment of a national advisory committee as recommended in our amendment. "It would be", he said, "an evasion of governmental responsibility", and this from a government which has set up more committees and commissions in order to evade responsibility for action than any other government in our history and has gone so far, in the hope of evading responsibility, as to promise committees which it does not get around to setting up. This proposed commission, if and when it is set up, is being used in order to remove from the government any responsibility for changes in the civil service which may be considered necessary in the interests of the economy.
However, when we advocate a national advisory board as a permanent agency to give counsel and advice to the government, expert advice and guidance, so that the government might discharge its responsibilities more efficiently, the minister says we cannot do this; it would be an invasion of responsibility. It is impossible to imagine a more flimsy, more ridiculous reason for rejecting a motion of this kind.
Some years ago, Benjamin Franklin is reported to have said this:
When men are employed, they are best contented; for on the days they worked they were

good-natured and cheerful, and, with the consciousness of having done a good day's work, they spent the evening jollily; but on our idle days they were mutinous and quarrelsome-
The dignity of man is enhanced by honest labour. We have a responsibility to allow each and every Canadian to earn a living and to justify his existence. This is a responsibility which must be faced, and which this government has refused to face from month to month. This evasion of responsibility is not based upon lack of advice.
More than 25 suggestions were enumerated by members of the Liberal party earlier this session, and what results have we seen? Not one of those suggestions has been acted upon. Why do the ministers not rise in their places and say that at least they will try, at least they will implement some of the suggestions in order to determine if something worth while cannot be done? This is not the course the present government follows. It has abdicated its responsibilities to hundreds of thousands of Canadians; it has allowed a situation to continue which has affected the good name of our country abroad. This has resulted in a lessening of the desire of immigrants to come to this country. It has affected our national and international credit; it has affected the regard in which we are held.
We urge, Mr. Speaker, that the government accept our proposal which has been put forward in good faith. The situation cries out for action, action which is the responsibility of this government to the people who elected it just three short years ago.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR VESTING OF PENSION RIGHTS
REQUEST FOR VESTING OF PENSION RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring up a grievance, and it is that for the most part there are no vesting rights in industrial pension schemes in vogue in our country. When I say this I realize that the employee can recover his contributions if there is termination of service before the pension matures; but for the most part he cannot benefit from the contributions made on his behalf by his employer. He has no right at all to any part of those contributions.
I have had representations many times from workmen in my area, and I know that early in March when I was away from this house representations were made to the government, to all members of the House of Commons and to members of the cabinet in respect to these pensions, and also in respect to a restoration of the pension vesting provisions of the Income Tax Act.
That prompted a question by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the Prime Minister said, in effect, that consideration was being given to these representations and that when a decision had been made it would be communicated to the house. There were other supplementary questions asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West, by the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Har-die) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) concerning the deletion of paragraph 10 (b) from the blue book. This deletion was published in the Canada Gazette of July 18, 1959. Whether that deletion was by order in council or by some other order I am not aware, and I do not know whether that order has ever been tabled.
I have brought up this question of the vesting of pension rights before in this house and I will not give all the reasons why I think this is very desirable. Most industrial pensions in our country mature after 20 or 25 years, and I do not think it is right that an employee has to work up to the very last day in order to get any part of his pension. Through misadventure or through sickness he might lose his pension by just a few days or a few months; and I have seen a case where it has been lost because his service fell short of the term by something less than one month.
With earlier pension rights I think it might be easy to work out portable pensions. It would be easier for a skilled man to get employment after he reaches the age of 40. Because of these pension plans, at the present time it is very hard for him to get employment in any trade. When he goes to apply he is generally turned down because he would become a liability owing to the pension 79951-0-265J
24, I960	4205
Request for Vesting of Pension Rights plan and therefore the employer will not hire him. I know that in the province of Ontario the suggestion has been made that there could be portable pensions, but I think that here we should have uniformity in relation to these pensions across the country.
I think the federal government might constitutionally, through the provisions of the Income Tax Act, provide for earlier vesting. I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said this matter came under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but the Income Tax Act comes under the jurisdiction of the federal government, and I believe the federal government could provide that there should be earlier vesting. If earlier vesting was not allowed by the employer the right of the employer to deduct contributions from his income tax could be disallowed in whole or in part.

speechtext:
I am
sure all members of this house regardless of party are pleased to see the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) back in good health to carry on his old fight on pension vesting. I know the hon. member has taken a long time interest in this problem. I think his first efforts in this direction were made in 1955, if I remember correctly, and although he was unfortunately absent through illness this session he continued to take an interest in this question as one could see by the resolution appearing on the order paper in his name this session.
I also represent a constituency which includes many workers who have been very interested in this question for a number of years. In 1950 the government distributed a blue book which established principles for pension vesting as related to the Income Tax Act, and according to those principles it was stated in the book:
The rights provided by employer contributions must vest in the employee within a determinable period, and particularly on the attainment by the employee of an age which would prejudice him m the event of severance from employment. Therefore, vesting should be absolute upon attainment oi age 50, subject to a minimum period, not exceeding 20 years of service or participation.
That is a very important clause of the pension vesting principles established in the blue book in 1950.
It was in 1955 that the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers was the first union in Canada to recognize the fact that the government was not applying the principles as established in the blue book. As a consequence the union made representations at that time to the former minister of finance and to the former minister of national revenue as well as to other members of the cabinet, and the matter was then taken into consideration. It was under consideration for a good
4206	HOUSE OF
Request for Vesting of Pension Rights length of time without any decision being announced. Then the present government came into office, and further representations were made. The government representatives agreed with the union that the matter should receive further consideration. Members of the union and some employers' organizations waited almost with bated breath the decision of the government on this question. However, they were disappointed when on July 18 of last year they read in the Canada Gazette new regulations with respect to the principles of pension vesting which in effect cancelled the former requirements.
I think I should explain that in brief all that pension vesting means is that if an employer is to get certain concessions with respect to his income tax in return for establishing a pension fund he must provide his employees with certain vested rights and interest in their pensions. Following the news published in the Gazette of July 18, 1959, further representations were made by local 598 of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers. Members of this local, together with some of the national officers, met some members of the cabinet and, I think, the president of local 598 met the Prime Minister personally and had a discussion with him on this matter of such importance to the union. In addition, the Canadian congress of labour made representations supporting the principles of pension vesting and urged the government to establish those principles in the income tax regulations.
Then the International Nickel Company made representations to the government in which it opposed the principles of pension vesting and the proposal that they should be included in the income tax regulations with respect to pension plans. In fact, the company was of the opinion that such rights should be established as a result of the processes of collective bargaining. Once again the members of the government told representatives from the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers that further consideration should be given to this question of vesting rights with respect to pension plans established by corporations and companies. The union has waited a long time for a decision. As the hon. member for Welland has mentioned, I asked the Prime Minister some time ago when a decision might be expected on this important issue, and the right hon. gentleman replied to the effect that when a decision was made it would be announced. Since then we have continued to wait for this announcement.
Then during the discussion of some of the income tax resolutions I raised the matter
[Mr. Herridge.I

again briefly. I think at the time I did something very unusual for me Mr. Speaker-I was slightly out of order. Anyway, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) replied to my inquiry and indicated that this was a provincial responsibility, because civil and property rights come within the jurisdiction of the provinces. We know that civil and property rights come within provincial jurisdiction but we claim, as did the representatives of the union, that when this government gives certain exemptions from income tax to corporations who set up certain funds for pensions purposes, it has the right to specify that the exemptions shall be related to certain responsibilities and obligations toward the employees; in this particular case, the vesting of pensions. That is definitely within the jurisdiction of the federal government and it was recognized as being so by the previous government and also by the present government in listening to representations on this question by unions and employers.
I wish to bring to the attention of this house that there seems to have been a great departure in government policy compared with that which was indicated by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) on November 7, 1957. I want to read a letter which the Minister of Labour wrote at that time to Mr. LeRoy L. Brown, 1110 W. 8th Avenue, Vancouver, 9, B.C. This is what the Minister of Labour had to say:

Mr. Speaker, I rise not to make any statement of decision on this matter for, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated on a previous occasion, it is a matter under study. I shall confine my remarks tonight simply to certain factual statements by way of setting forth the problem for a better understanding of it, if I may do so.
The fact is that parliament has no jurisdiction to provide for vesting of pension rights. This is obviously a matter falling within the sphere of property and civil rights and is a matter strictly under provincial jurisdiction. Some of the provincial governments have already been examining the question. It may be recalled by hon. members that at the recent session of the legislature of Ontario there was discussion of this matter and the legislature on motion of the government there established a committee to study this question. That study, according to my information, is proceeding. Evidence is being taken on it and the counsel of experts has already been sought on the subject. With respect to jurisdiction it is a matter beyond question that this is something lying outside the jurisdiction of parliament. The only way in which it has at any time become a matter of federal consideration has been in relation to the provisions of the Income Tax Act.
As all hon. members are aware, the act makes provision for deduction from income in the case of both employers and employees of certain payments made to pension funds. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) has referred to the situation that followed 1950. At that time regulations were issued, of which the hon. gentleman made mention, on the assumption that it was within the power of the government under the provisions of the Income Tax Act to say that the right to deduct these pension payments should be limited to cases where certain rights, in the clause that he mentioned, were preserved.
I must point out in the first place that that was interpreted in the government departments concerned as applicable only to pensions of a contributory nature. In other words, it was deemed applicable to those to which both the employer and employee contributed. It was interpreted as not having

Request for Vesting of Pension Rights any application at all to pension funds established only at the instance of the employer to which the employee made no contribution.
Another development occurred not long after. Because of the multiplicity of these pension funds and the very great variety of them it was found to be quite impossible to undertake a review of all the pensions plans and to determine whether in every case under the terms of the trust created there was a vesting or a compliance with the provisions of the regulation. It became a physical impossibility. Some few years ago any attempt at a detailed review of these trust documents was given up. That was before we came into office. There are literally thousands of these plans.
The hon. member for Kootenay West spoke of the issuance of the new blue book as though that made some change in the situation. It really did not. It did not make any change in the situation at all. It was recognized that this was something under the then existing circumstances that was quite incapable of enforcement and, indeed, it was concluded that it was beyond the powers conferred by the act to attempt to impose or enforce such a condition. It is quite clear, therefore, that the regulations which appeared in the Canada Gazette last July made no change in the situation. They simply took account of an existing fact, a fact which had already been in existence for several years in the practice that had been followed. Therefore I wish to make it quite clear that no change in this respect has in fact occurred since the present government came into office.
The hon. member for Kootenay West spoke of the desirability of providing for transferability of pension contributions. I wonder whether he has overlooked the amendment introduced into the Income Tax Act at the 1959 session on a government resolution that made just that kind of provision. You will find that in section 11, subsection 1, paragraph (u) of the Income Tax Act. It makes clear provision for the transferability of these pension contributions so far as parliament can so provide in enacting taxing legislation within the ambit of the federal powers.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I emphasize that I have not risen to announce any policy in this respect. I have risen simply to indicate certain facts to the house in the hope that they may contribute to a clearer understanding of the situation, of the limitations that affect the federal authority in this respect, and of the fact there is an indication that the provincial legislatures and governments are carefully examining this question since it is only in that quarter that provision can


be made that will effect the right of vesting in such funds as between employers, employees and trustees of such funds.
As the Prime Minister indicated on an earlier occasion, this subject is complex. It has received and is receiving very careful study. Some hon. members may regret that it is as complex or that the federal powers are as limited as they are in this respect, but they are the facts and whatever consideration can be given to this question must be given within the kind of limits I have indicated.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the discussion of this very important subject. I was interested in hearing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) state that portable pensions are not a matter of federal jurisdiction. I maintain, however, that the federal government has some responsibility in the matter of pensions and the provision of a general pension plan acceptable in every part of Canada. If that is the case, then it has got to be a federal proposition and not merely a matter of provincial jurisdiction.
One of the major problems facing workers in industry today is the difficulty of men over 40 getting another job if for some reason their previous job comes to an end. As everyone knows, the acceleration of technological change has hit the hardest at older workers who have been displaced by machines. Many of these displaced workers were participants in pension schemes of all kinds, as intimated by the Minister of Finance, but their prospects for security are threatened through loss of employment. As a result, people 45 years of age and over find it extremely difficult to get a job in industries that have their own pension plans which in many instances preclude the hiring of men

and women over 40. The only fair solution to this problem, and it is a serious problem, is a measure or method, call it what you will, which would permit an employee to change his job without affecting his pension plan. I have an article here written by Mr. Cecil G. White, a fellow of the society of actuaries and an employee in the department of insurance. I think it is a very important article and I wish to read from it. It has this to say in part:
Why is it so important for the employee who changes jobs to preserve the pensions he earns with a succession of employers? There are several reasons, but the one that concerns us today is the effect this will have on his chances of employment in the future.
Many employers may be unwilling to hire an older worker who has no pension credits from previous employments. Quite naturally, these employers wish to avoid the embarrassment and bad public relations that may arise if they should be obliged to retire such an employee before he has had time to earn an adequate pension.
The two alternative possibilities are to keep the employee in service beyond the time when he is really effective or to bear the cost of supplementing his pension, but both of these involve added expense for the employers and are therefore unattractive. These considerations appear to be among the most important obstacles associated in the minds of employers with the hiring of otherwise qualified older workers.
This may or may not be an ideal solution but it is an attempt to alleviate discrimination against older workers. I am sure that the proposal advanced in the article will be of interest to every member of the house. I continue:
Well, now, here we have a serious problem. A pension plan with all its advantages for a firm's employees seems to have the disadvantage of raising a barrier against the hiring of some older people. Is this really the situation? In a sense it is, but perhaps it would be more correct to say that each of them has built up his own barrier during his years of previous employment by his failure to preserve his pension credits.
One remedy for this lies in making it possible for those employees who leave an employer after a reasonable period of service to keep the pension credits that they have earned. How can this be done? One method that seems obvious, but like many obvious methods involves some technical difficulties, is to transfer the employee's rights under one plan into the plan of his next employer.
Now, the income tax amendment mentioned by the Minister of Finance a moment ago was designed to facilitate some transfers.
To date, however, such "portable pension credits", as some people call them, are used only sparingly in Canada, being found most commonly in plans for government employees.
Other attempts to preserve the pension credits of employees who change jobs have been made through the mechanism of industry-wide pension plans. Under such a plan, an employee may move from one employer to another within the industry and always retain his earned pension. However, this arrangement can benefit an employee only as long as he stays within the industry, so that even an industry-wide plan is limited in its application.

Most employees who change jobs in Canada do so without the benefit of either a system of "portable pension credits" or an industry-wide plan. How do they make out in their efforts to preserve the pensions they have earned with a succession of employers? Any attempt to answer this question must take account of two main factors in Canadian pension plans-the vesting formulas and the optional forms of benefit available on voluntary termination of service.
The vesting formula determines the conditions under which the employee acquires a right to part or all of the contributions made by the employer on his behalf. The employee always retains a fully vested right to his own contributions, but his entitlement to the benefit arising from the employer's contributions depends on his length of service or sometimes on the number of years he has participated in the plan.
There is great variety in the vesting provisions of Canadian pension plans. Plans paid for entirely by the employer frequently have no provision for vesting any rights in a separating employee, except at retirement age.
I must point out, Mr. Speaker, that very many of these plans are such now that they are paid by the employer. However, the employee always retains a full and vested right to his own contribution.
Of the pension plans to which the employees contribute, comparatively few give full vesting before the completion of 15 years of service. Some plans have a formula that provides gradual vesting. Under these, the proportion of the employer's contributions that vests in the employee, increases year by year until the full amount is vested.
A typical formula gives the employee a vested right to 10 per cent of the employer's contributions after 10 years of service, with an additional 10 per cent being granted each year thereafter, so that full vesting is achieved on completion of 19 years of service.
A very few plans in Canada provide that the employer's contributions vest in the employee as soon as they are paid, regardless of the employee's age, service or participation in the plan. Such plans offer no restriction on the mobility of the employee. If the occasion arises for him to seek other employment, he is always in the favourable position of having pension credits.
From this brief description of the vesting provisions in Canadian pension plans, you can see that it is seldom possible for an employee who changes jobs to build up pension credits for his service with each employer. From this point of view, the present situation with respect to vesting in pension plans is less than satisfactory.

I believe it is very important that these vesting rights in the pension plan be immediate and that a worker working in an industry for any length of time should have an initial period through which he would have to work before he became a full time employee. It has to do with the operation of the national employment service as it affects constituencies where the commission has no offices and where there is a rather high degree of seasonal unemployment, as unhappily, there is in my constituency.
I do not want anything I say to be misinterpreted as the slightest criticism of the personnel of the unemployment insurance commission who, I think, are conscientiously doing a very good job under great difficulties in every part of Canada with which I have 79951-0-266 J

Operations of Employment Offices anything to do. What I am talking about is the system itself, and I am not saying, either, that it is the fault of Her Majesty's present advisers, though this is a grievance against the government because it is something which I feel ought to be changed in the circumstances.
So that I can save the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell), the pain of asking me why we did not change it, let me say that whether we should have changed it or not, we did not change it. We are now in 1960 and the power to change this is vested for the time being-and not for very long -in someone else. Those people will be judged not by what we did before 1957 or by what we left undone before 1957 but what they have done, or left undone since 1957. Because I do not want to make this controversial, I intend to appeal to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr)-and I trust someone will carry my appeal to him-to get the commission to do something about this question.
The problem is this: once a person has exhausted his unemployment insurance benefits there is at the present time little or no real incentive for him, particularly in the winter months when there is practically no employment available in many parts of the country, to keep his name on the registers of the employment service. Means are provided for his doing so if he wishes, and the commission always shows the greatest possible courtesy if he does so, but there is a tendency for those who are unemployed to let their names drop off these registers. I can understand, also, that the staff do not want to keep a lot of deadwood on the list, and they should not. I make no criticism of that.
This does mean, however, that a great many people who are unemployed, and who in many cases, have been longer employed than a great many others who are getting insurance benefits, are denied the opportunity of hearing about such jobs as may be available simply because they do live in outlying places and are not readily accessible to the offices. This is a difficult problem. I do not think there is an easy solution to it; if there were it would no doubt have been solved long ago. But it is a problem. The national employment offices exist to serve all Canadians and not just those who happen for the time being to be drawing benefits.
I do not think the commission or its employees consciously tend to bring job opportunities to the attention primarily of those who are drawing benefit rather than to others, but I suggest that unconsciously it does happen that way, because those persons who are

Operations of Employment Offices on the list are more readily available and because it is easier to bring matters of that kind to their notice.
I feel that some device should be found for maintaining a priority in the offering of these jobs, and that it should be the exact opposite of the usual rules of seniority which one readily understands. But in the case of a national employment service, surely the job should be offered first to those who have been unemployed the longest and not to those who lost their jobs the most recently.
In urban communities this may not be a very great problem. In urban communities where there is an employment office in the community where an unemployed person even if he no longer has benefits can without very much effort on his part see that his name is kept on the list, a man can be informed of job opportunities without too much trouble. But when you live, as do many of my constituents, 100 or 200 miles from the nearest office, when job opportunities do turn up it is often necessary to make rather complicated inquiries by the postal service which is not as good, I am sorry to say, in many parts of my riding, as it is in metropolitan Montreal.
Again I am making no criticism on that account, but it is one of those facts. I do think more attention should be given to establishing some practical and workable means to ensure that those unemployed persons who are driven on to relief because their benefits have expired are given an opportunity- indeed, I would say, a priority-with regard to learning about opportunities for employment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to support the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and express my appreciation for his bringing up the subject. In the matter of obtaining employment my constituents are handicapped to an even greater extent than his are.
I should like to make it very clear at the beginning that I have no criticism whatever to make of the officials of the unemployment insurance commission. I have nothing but good to say about them. They are doing a difficult job well. My criticism is, if anything, against geography. I know that this government despite its power cannot alter the shape of the physical properties of Canada but I do think it should take these physical characteristics into consideration in making decisions as to who should have jobs and when.
As hon. members know, although my constituency takes in central Newfoundland it extends all down the east side of the great northern peninsula and includes all of Labrador. Many of my constituents live a long way

from the unemployment offices at St. John's, Grand Falls and Corner Brook. Communications are slow and unless there is some policy adopted whereby available jobs are divided up regionally I cannot see how the men in remote areas will have a fair chance of obtaining employment in competition with those who live in the vicinity of the employment offices.
I am not sure that the establishment of more employment offices would be a satisfactory answer. I do think there should be more field men provided and the residence of those making application for jobs should be taken into consideration by those who have it in their power to grant employment.
In my own district there is seasonal unemployment. At this time of year when work grows more plentiful and there are a number of jobs offered the people living, for instance, in north White Bay are definitely handicapped compared to those living in more populous areas, but those who live in remote districts should have an equal opportunity of earning much-needed income during the period of employment.
I would hope a policy would be adopted whereby those who live in remote areas would be given opportunities of employment equal with those living near the employment offices at St. John's, Grand Falls and Corner Brook. If such a policy were instituted it would mean that many men would have employment this summer and would be able to support their families. On the whole I believe it would create a better feeling of satisfaction among the people in many parts of my riding and indeed in all the remote areas of Newfoundland and Labrador. There does appear to be a reasonable opportunity in Newfoundland this year for a number of people to be placed in employment. I think it would be nothing short of tragic if the greater number of these jobs were filled from one or two areas instead of being spread all over the island and Labrador where some of this employment will take place.
From recent letters and telegrams I have received I know that the people in northern Newfoundland feel they are not receiving a fair chance to obtain work when it is offered. I urge the government to give this matter careful and sympathetic consideration now because with the season advancing there is a considerable amount of urgency. Unless a decision is made now and such a policy put into effect immediately it will be too late to bring about a fair distribution of employment in Newfoundland and Labrador this year.

However, there is not much time in which to discuss this important subject. For the purposes of the record I should like to point out that there are two policies in existence which would be contrary to the proposal advanced.
In the first place Canadian National Railways in the maritimes has a policy under which preference must be given to laid-off former C.N.R. employees. There are also many municipalities that give preference to local residents especially in the winter works programs. The policy suggested would encourage people to remain on benefits even though there might be an opportunity of work because it was proposed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) that preference should be given by the national employment service to people who had been on benefits for the longest period of time.
